'''''Chara vulgaris''''', also called the '''common stonewort''',<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |access-date=2014-10-17 }}</ref> is a species of [[charophyte]] green alga. It is one of the most widespread species of the genus ''[[Chara (alga)|Chara]]'' and occurs across much of Europe, Asia, Africa, North America, and Australia.

The [[thallus]] of ''Chara vulgaris'' is macroscopic and highly organized, consisting of a main axis differentiated into nodes and elongated [[internode (botany)|internode]]s. At each node, a whorl of branchlets is produced. The organism is anchored to the substrate by [[rhizoids]]. The species is relatively polymorphic in its organization.

The species is of ecological importance in aquatic environments. It is particularly common in alkaline waters rich in [[calcium bicarbonate]] (CaCO<sub>3</sub>) and can tolerate moderate [[eutrophication]], although dense populations are often associated with relatively clear water conditions.

== Description ==
''Chara vulgaris'' is a medium-sized stonewort that typically reaches up to 50 cm in length. The [[thallus]] is usually greyish-green to green in colour and is often moderately encrusted with [[calcium carbonate]]. The main axis is corticated, with a cortex consisting of a primary cortical row and a single secondary row between adjacent primary rows (diplostichous).<ref name="flora">{{cite book | editor1-last = John | editor1-first = DM | editor2-last = Whitton | editor2-first = BA | editor3-last = Brook | editor3-first = AJ | title=The freshwater algal flora of the British Isles | publisher = Cambridge University Press | date=2005 | isbn = 978-0-521-77051-4 | page = 602}}</ref>

Spine cells are generally small and solitary, although they may become elongated. When well developed, these spine cells are often pressed against the axis and appear to lie within the grooves formed by the cortical rows, a condition known as [[aulacanthy]]. The species is highly variable, however, and some forms may show cortical rows of nearly equal width (isostichous).<ref name="flora" />

== Ecology ==
''C. vulgaris'' can form extensive underwater meadows that provide habitat for invertebrates, refuge for fish larvae, and feeding grounds for [[waterfowl]]. Dense stands reduce sediment resuspension and can improve water clarity by competing with [[phytoplankton]] for nutrients.<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Kufel | first1=Lech | last2=Kufel | first2=Irena | title=Chara beds acting as nutrient sinks in shallow lakes—a review | journal=Aquatic Botany | volume=72 | issue=3-4 | date=2002 | doi=10.1016/S0304-3770(01)00204-2 | pages=249–260}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Van den Berg M, Scheffer M, Coops H | title=The role of characean algae in the management of eutrophic shallow lakes | journal=Journal of Phycology | volume=34 | pages= 750–756 | date=1998}}</ref> Because of these ecological functions, charophyte communities are used as indicators of freshwater ecosystem quality. ''C. vulgaris'' has been evaluated for its [[phytoremediation]] potential.<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Kufel | first1=Lech | last2=Kufel | first2=Irena | title=Chara beds acting as nutrient sinks in shallow lakes—a review | journal=Aquatic Botany | volume=72 | issue=3-4 | date=2002 | doi=10.1016/S0304-3770(01)00204-2 | pages=249–260 | url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0304377001002042 | access-date=2026-05-28| url-access=subscription }}</ref> 

=== Distribution ===
The species is widely distributed and occurs throughout much of the world in freshwater habitats, including [[pond]]s, [[ditch]]es, [[littoral]] pools and periodic waters. The alga can grow down to one meter deep. ''C. vulgaris'' is also known to survive in moderately saline conditions.<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Winter | first1=U. | last2=Kirst | first2=G. O. | title=Salinity response of a freshwater charophyte, Chara vulgaris | journal=Plant, Cell & Environment | volume=13 | issue=2 | date=1990 | issn=0140-7791 | doi=10.1111/j.1365-3040.1990.tb01284.x | pages=123–134 | url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1365-3040.1990.tb01284.x | access-date=2026-05-28| url-access=subscription }}</ref>

== Reproduction ==
The reproductive organs of ''C. vulgaris'' are among the most structurally complex found in algae. The species is [[monoecious]], bearing both male and female [[gametangia]] on the same individual.<ref name="flora" /> The spherical orange-red structures are [[antheridia]], which produce multiflagellate sperm cells, while the adjacent elongated [[oogonia]] contain a single egg cell. Following fertilization, a resistant oospore is formed that can survive adverse environmental conditions and germinate when conditions improve. Reproductivity is highest in early summer, but can start as early as February in warmer regions.<ref>{{cite book |editor1-last=Schubert |editor1-first=H |editor2-last=Blindow |editor2-first=I |editor3-last=Nat |editor3-first=E |title=Charophytes of Europe |date=2024 |publisher=Springer |isbn=978-3-031-31898-6|page=706}}</ref>
